text:
Is this game great? Its awesome! Would I recommend buying it? Unfortunately, not right now.

Manor Lords is truly something special. No one has ever made a game quite like this before. Its approach is completely different from anything we know from other city builders. It feels real, authentic, and organic, while offering interesting and unique mechanics. The graphics are beautiful, and the potential for the future is enormous. However, new players should stay away from it for now because this game gives you the feeling of being in a toxic relationship.

It's not that the developers took the money and went on an endless vacation. Quite the opposite! The team puts a tremendous amount of effort into optimization, bug fixes, and countless small improvements that may seem insignificant at first glance but make a huge difference when combined. But how good are 1000 bug fixes if we've received almost no new content in the last two years? We've only had 2.5 truly good content updates: the Manor update, the AI villages (which, in my opinion, work terribly, but it's still nice to see something "alive" on the map that wasn't created by the player), and the Tier 3 houses. And that's about it. Yes, we've also received new maps, but that's not what we're waiting for.

And that's exactly the problem: the patient has been in a coma for two years now. His condition is stable, but he's still in a coma.

If you look at the cover art of Manor Lords, you'll see a beautiful medieval city in the background. But at the current pace of development, we might not get there for another ten years. There is still so much content missing from this game. I think we've only received about 30% of what we should have by now. And I'm not even talking about all the missing mechanics.

I wish I could build a large, beautiful stone city. I wish we would get more story in the game, engage in meaningful politics on both a regional and local level, and be forced to make decisions with both positive and terrible consequences. Who knows, maybe even have the opportunity to become king and turn our region into the capital. I wish we had mounted military units, barracks, and so much more, along with a more complex economy. And I know this studio is capable of delivering all of that. But at the current pace, GTA 7 will probably be released first, and that's a really big problem.

Until more starts happening, until we begin receiving new content on a regular basis, I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone. We're already on version 0.8.9, almost at a full release, yet it still feels more like version 0.5.

But ArrowHead and Sony need to tread lightly with their greed. Right now, they are trampling their playerbase. It's a $40 game with micro-transactions adding up to $300+, if you want to unlock everything. You can get everything without buying any micro-transactions, if you're willing to [i]grind[/i] for hundreds of hours.

ArrowHead trying to stop super credit cheaters is understandable. It is their bottom-line, after all. But they shouldn't frame it as if everyone demanded they stop them. ArrowHead is treating the symptom, not the disease. Instead of focusing on super credit cheaters, why not fix the reason people want to super credit cheat in the first place? [b]Make late-game progression fun. Fix super credit farming/grinding.[/b] Lower prices of old warbonds, increase spawn rates of super credits on high level missions (instead of decreasing, because of rare samples being added to the spawn pool), add more spawn points for super credits, or reward super credits for missions / major orders / galactic campaigns, etc. Ideally, discourage players from "farming"/"grinding" and encourage them to play the game. Why do I have to say this out loud?!? ArrowHead has so many options. Any of these changes would mean good PR, keeping concurrent players recommending the game and new / future players engaged with a good progression system. More players = more money. People who buy super credits aren't going to stop if super credit "farming" is made easier, just like how super credit cheaters aren't going to stop because you "crack down" on them. You already have kernel-level anti-cheat. They found ways around that, they'll find ways around this. I'd buy the super citizen edition, if ArrowHead would address these longstanding problems.

I've already done the grinding. New players should have the option of [b]NOT[/b] [i]grinding[/i] for [b]HUNDREDS[/b] of hours to unlock everything. They should be able to earn SC at a reasonable rate while playing the game casually.

text:
I played this game mostly coop with 3 other friends of mine.

This is one of those games that I started out enjoying, but then I reached a certain point where I didn't want to play it anymore.  So for those who don't know, this is essentially a 3D auto-running platformer.  There's a hub world that is free roam where you can pick which shard (world) to play through and places to buy permanent upgrades, traversal items that you can use, cosmetics, etc using anti-sparks (this game's currency which you get by beating a shard).  When you select a shard, you play through a series of levels until you get to the boss, which you must defeat without losing all your lives (you start with 3 but can upgrade to 4).  

The levels range from "race to the end", "race to the end extra hard mode" (where the level itself is harder, but you are rewarded with an item that can aid you), "shops where you can buy items with sparks (this game's other currency) you collect from other levels", "rest areas where you restore health and regain a life", and "encounters which can result in you gaining an item or doing a challenge which rewards you with sparks".  When you enter a shard, a random assortment of those kinds of levels are determined and laid out in branching paths that all lead to the boss level.  So while the available levels are determined at random, the path you take to the boss is entirely up to you.

About the race levels, the idea is that the level is collapsing and you need to reach the end without dying.  You die by losing all your health, which can happen by running into obstacles, running into lasers or explosions, falling into a bottomless pit (instant death), or staying in a "collapsed" part of the level.  In order to outrun the collapse, you have to maintain your speed/boost your speed by making sure you land your jumps perfectly (so you don't stumble), not colliding into anything, going through boost rings, using items you get from other levels (like the shop levels), or using 1 of 4 available traversal items you can acquire in the hub world.  There's also sparks for you to collect as you run through the level, and depending on what your rating is after you reach the end, you'll get a certain amount of sparks for completing the level.

When you play online, only 1 person has to make it to the end and beat the boss for the shard to be cleared for everyone (and everyone gets the same amount of anti-sparks).  Also, if one or more of your friends loses all of their lives, if you go to a "rest area" level, they'll regain 1 of their lives.  Playing with friends on the 2 different "race" kinds of levels involves each of you racing to the end on the same level (meaning you see everyone) but you can't interact with them physically (so you don't have to worry about colliding with them).  Also, the sparks available to collect in the race levels are unique to each player, so you're not all gunning  for the same sparks.  Now, as for the shop worlds, the items available for purchase is shared.  So for example, if Player 1 buys Item 1, then that means none of the other players can buy Item 1, and only Player 1 has that specific Item 1.  Items available for purchase are determined in groups of 3, and if you want to generate a new group of available items, someone has to pay sparks to do that.  Lastly, boss levels are like the race levels in that you're all playing on the same level and can see each other, but you can't collide with anyone.  But you're all trying to take down the same boss.

If you're playing by yourself and you lose a life on a race level, then you have to start the race again from the beginning (there are no checkpoints).  However, if you're playing with friends online, only 1 player has to make it to the end for everyone to progress to the next level, and you only have to restart the race level from the beginning if every player dies on the level.  Same sort of logic for boss levels.  Say for example the boss has 3 HP.  If you're fighting the boss by yourself (offline), and you damage the boss twice, if the boss kills you first, then you have to start the fight from the beginning (meaning the boss has 3 HP again).  Contrast that with playing with friends (online).  If a player damages the boss once and then everyone loses a life, then all players with available lives spawn back in and the boss only has 2 HP left.  So in a way, its like the game is more balanced to playing online then offline.

Regarding the permanent upgrades you can buy with anti-sparks, those include increasing your health, increasing your energy (which you use to activate a traversal item), increasing the amount of lives you have (though you can only increase it to 4 in total), increasing the amount of sparks you have at the start of a shard, increasing the amount of sparks available in a level to collect, and increasing the rarity of the items that spawn in the shop levels.

So what were the things that killed the enjoyment of the game for everyone?  The main one was the difficulty spikes.  It doesn't take long for this game's difficulty to suddenly jump (some say it was Shard 3 where the first spike happens).  I'm not kidding when I say you have to quickly get good at making sure ALL your landings are perfect, which is a lot easier said than done when the game starts having levels with insane obstacles and a lot of things that send your character into the air.  Also, eventually the game starts throwing "race levels" and "extra hard race levels" that have some kind of distortion.  Sometimes those distortions are helpful (like restoring health at the beginning of the level), but often times are detrimental (like halving your boost for the level or making you take double damage).  But even if you are perfect at landing your jumps AND you're not bombarded with a selection of difficult race levels in later shards, you still have to cross your fingers extra hard and pray that the items available to you in your run of the later shards are actually good.  Because if you get stuck with bad items in those later shards, it's basically impossible for you to win.  And since you can't permanent increase your speed or boost, you're completely reliant on the RNG providing you the CHANCE of getting items that can aid with that.

Another annoyance was that, outside of the final boss, this game only has 3 bosses, which each get re-used throughout the game.  Each time they get re-used, some mechanic about them is altered to make them more difficult to fight.  So it was disappointing to see them cheap out on the bosses.

If you're wondering why I haven't mentioned the story, its because it's not much of one to comment on.  Its about as interesting and deep as one you'd find in a Sonic game, and its mostly brought across via static drawings of the characters talking about it.  So in short, the story is there and that's all there is to say about it.

I was only able to get to Shard 8 of 10 before I called it quits as it felt like I was completely beholden to the RNG at that point.  And losing because less because you suck at the game and more because the game dealt you a bad hand isn't what I call at good time.  So while there was initial enjoyment, the more we played, the less fun we had.

text:
I left Elite Dangerous about eight years ago because of engineering. What should have been an optional progression system became a mandatory grind that turned ship building into a second job instead of something fun. I recently decided to give the game another chance, hoping years of updates had addressed those problems.

Instead, I found that nearly everything about the game feels like trying to run a footrace underwater.

Engineering is still effectively mandatory if you want to participate in combat without being hopelessly outclassed. The catch? To get the materials needed for engineering, you're often pushed into fighting enemies who are already engineered while you have none of the upgrades yourself. It's a ridiculous progression loop that punishes you for not already having what you're trying to unlock.

Then there's the travel. Want to engineer your weapons? Fly several hundred light-years to one engineer. Need shields next? Fly several hundred more to another NPC. Thrusters? Repeat the process. Instead of playing the game, you're spending hours staring at a jump counter.

Nothing respects your time.

The information overload doesn't help. Every system seems buried beneath multiple layers of menus, submenus, and obscure interfaces. Even after completing the tutorials, the game barely explains its mechanics. You're left searching through third-party websites, YouTube videos, and community spreadsheets just to understand systems that should be explained in-game.

Preparation has become the game.

You spend more time gathering materials, flying across the galaxy, unlocking engineers, pinning blueprints, hunting down obscure resources, and configuring modules than actually doing the activities you logged in to enjoy. Whether it's combat, exploration, or bounty hunting, the setup feels ten times longer than the payoff.

And here's the thing: the game isn't difficult.

It's not challenging in the satisfying sense. It's unfair, convoluted, and intentionally time-consuming. Artificial barriers aren't the same thing as meaningful gameplay.

To make matters worse, the technical state of the game feels surprisingly rough. Within five to ten minutes of logging in, I can almost guarantee I'll encounter some kind of bug—overlapping ship menus, interface glitches, or a black screen after disembarking. These aren't rare edge cases; they happen often enough that they become part of the expected experience.

It gives the impression that Frontier is doing the absolute bare minimum required to keep the game functional because there isn't a true MMO space sim competitor pushing them to improve. Whether that's true or not, that's certainly how the game feels.

The saddest part is that I wanted to like it.

The flight model is still fantastic. The galaxy is still beautiful. Flying your ship still captures a sense of scale that few games can match. But all of that potential is buried beneath layers of unnecessary friction and endless busywork.

I honestly don't understand how brand-new players stick with this game. Without engineering, you're routinely matched against opponents that vastly outclass you. Yet acquiring engineering materials often requires surviving exactly those encounters. It's a progression system that borders on self-parody.

Elite Dangerous doesn't feel like a game that's trying to entertain you. It feels like a game that's constantly testing how much inconvenience you'll tolerate before giving up.
label: negative

text:
I love this game like a mother loves her ugly baby boy with down syndrome. As it develops, so do the birth defects. 

Internal affairs are quite good in my opinion. Garden your nation. Extract the resources you need to fuel your internal  market. Navigate around debt to maximise investment in order to develop faster than your neighbours. Process resources in factories to industrialize. Innovate to increase efficiency. Educate the populace. Increase standards of living. Attempt to turn a conservative agricultural society into a liberal industrial powerhouse before compromising with labour movements so that unnecessary revolts do not disrupt production.

War is where the game becomes NOT fun, at least to me. While the front system prevents cheesing the war AI, it quickly becomes a frustrating mess. While it is not as bad as a few years ago (armies could teleport across the world), war fronts are often in nonsensical locations. Playing as Greece vs France, I bordered them in Northern Africa and Italy. The game decided the only front was in Africa. Some time into the war, it suddenly decided there was a front in Italy after all. 
Navies actually have a use now and the redesigned interest system means a random European tiny nation cannot suddenly conquert the African East coast in 5 years. 
Starting a war can be the most frustrating experience of all. See, you don't declare war. A diplomatic play starts when a nation demands something from another nation. If the defender refuses, a countdown starts. 21 to 79 days after the refusal, more demands can be added by both the attacker and defender and other nations can be persuaded to join either side. During the war, nothing can be changed and nobody can join.
Is it better than before? Yes. Is it still bad? Yes. Victoria 2 had a wider unit variety. Perhaps it made things more complicating, but to me that is more fun than having 100 of the same regiment for infantry, artillery and cavalry.

My recommendation for newcomers is to always buy at a discount, and/or wait until the game is further developed. Fellow Paradox autist spreadsheet simulator enjoyers will keep playing and complaining until the game is in a better state (hopefully).

Boring, boring, boring.

I'm not a huge afficionado of "survivors" games but I've played and liked a few at this point, and this is easily my least favorite (of the ones that "made the cut" to be purchased/played). 

Moment to moment gameplay is just extremely boring. Run your character in circles to avoid enemy attacks. Make level up decisions every few seconds, though they tend to have an obvious best choice once you get a build going. The constant input required is not mentally engaging and makes me feel like a wide-eyed iPad baby. 

Meta-gameplay (progression, unlocks, buildcraft) reminds me of a demonetized mobile game. Instead of having complex systems to integrate microtransactions, it has similar, byzantine complexity for complexity's sake. There are obvious builds/unlocks/combos to work towards, but nothing mentally stimulating. It's more of a "that seems strong" than a "wow, neat!" 

I do really wish they would choose a design lane. Option one would be to turn off enemy ranged attacks/AOEs and turn it into a bullet heaven buildcraft game. Option two would be to slow down the level-ups, make enemy attacks harder to deal with and more reflex-based, and try to put some mental interest into combat. 

They're in whatever the opposite of a sweet spot is right now: neither the combat nor progression elements feel like they stand on their own, and each feels like an annoying interruption of the other.

p.s. the player character chatter is one of the dumbest things. It reminds me of Arnold Schwarzenegger's lines as Mr. Freeze in Batman & Robin. "Allow me to break the ice" "Stay cool" "A freeze is coming." Each character in game has a full rotation of similarly asinine, themed-to-a-fault lines. Gameplay with different characters feels roughly identical, which makes the chatter seem like a cringe attempt to make the characters seem distinct.

text:
[h1]A soulless monument to wasted potential[/h1]

[i]Disclaimer: I played it from a shared library. I don’t own the game myself.[/i]

I tried to like this game. I really did. Even though I played Skyrim more like a fantasy sim than an actual RPG and Fallout 4 as a settlement builder sim, I enjoyed them both. So I thought I would enjoy Starfield as well. I tried to ignore the negative reviews and to try it with an open mind. I kept playing. Every level I told myself “Maybe [i]now[/i] it would get fun and interesting.” It never did.

[h2]The Good:[/h2]

1. The sense of exploration is actually great… to a certain extent. I loved the planet hopping and watching how humanity tried to colonize different planets with different environments and how they face such different challenges everywhere. It makes you appreciate how vast and varied the galaxy is. It reminded me of Mass Effect and the Outer Worlds. But this feeling doesn't last. More on that later.

2. The level progression is a step in the right direction for Bethesda, in my opinion. Instead of it being fully usage-based like Elder Scrolls or fully experience-based like Fallout, they have tried a mix. You earn skill points via experience like traditional RPGs but you can’t use them until you have completed certain challenges relevant to that skill. This method stops ‘cheesing’ the difficulty (like spamming Illusion spells to level up) but also maintains the idea that you need to use a particular skill to get better at it.

And that’s it. These are the only two good things I had to say about the game.

[h2]The Bad:[/h2]

1. The game is procedurally generated hell. Remember how I wrote about how good exploration feels? It does, really. [i]However[/i], those carefully constructed locations are few and far between. I can understand why. We can’t expect Bethesda to hand-craft hundreds of different such locations. And so Bethesda approaches it differently from games like No Man’s Sky where [i]everything[/i] is generated. As a result, when you step out of such well-designed cities and start getting into random ‘civilian outposts’ or ‘abandoned facilities’ with nameless citizens and enemies, the contrast feels very jarring. The immersion breaks.

2. Space travel is boring as hell. Unlike No Man’s Sky, you can’t actually fly from planet to planet seamlessly. You can’t even land or launch manually. It’s all loading screens! And it’s largely pointless. Once you reach a destination, you can skip your ship entirely and just fast travel to it. The only times the ship has any relevance is during fights with enemy spaceships. Even then the controls are very clunky.

3. I’ve played an incredible amount of RPGs in my life, and so I’ve gotten used to good writing, interesting twists, incredible character depth. So when Starfield kept giving me simple fetch quests one after another, I was confused. Every time I thought, maybe [i]this time[/i] it would be something interesting and unexpected. But I was waiting for something that doesn’t exist.

Most of the quests (maybe 80% or more of what I did) are fetch quests- go there, do this menial task. You’ll be asked to deliver letters, birthday gifts, dinner plates, boots, and so on. I don’t mind the occasional fetch quests. They are a staple of the genre after all, but there are very few actually interesting quests in this game. It also doesn't help at all that most of the quests are radiant, i.e. they are procedurally generated.

4. It’s not just quests, the writing overall feels very mechanical and inconsistent, even by Bethesda’s standards. In Skyrim, I actually cared about some NPCs. Hadvar was my bro. I loved the quaint little village of Riverwood and its simple inhabitants. Granted that in Fallout 4 I did not care about my son, but I would have gone to war over Codsworth. In Starfield, the characters are incredibly generic and their personality has the depth of a tissue paper. They feel as soulless as the game. I myself never felt any sort of connection with any of them. Even the companions felt forced, drab, and out of place.

5.  My biggest gripe is probably with the inventory and the outpost systems. Usually I love inventory limit in video games. I enjoy managing the weight of items and making decisions about what to carry and what to leave behind. But Starfield takes that to an extreme. The sheer variety of resources you find in this game dwarfs Skyrim or Fallout 4, and they weigh [i]a lot[/i]. Even if you are not a hoarder, you will definitely struggle to carry the important things, and you will spend a lot of time encumbered. And why would you want to carry so much? That brings me to my next point.

6. Like I said, I did not much like Fallout 4 as an RPG, but I loved it as a settlement building simulator. The thrill you got from taking over an abandoned or vulnerable facility and turning it into a powerhouse was unparalleled. It also helped that you could give poor wasteland survivors a shelter and a purpose in your bases. The building system was simple and yet, elegant. In Starfield, however, it is neither.

You can’t drop your resources at the workbench anymore. You have to build storages and warehouses, which have very little space and fill up way too fast. You also can’t build simple caravan routes between your outposts. You have to create cargo links which can [i]only[/i] carry specific resources at a time. And since the resources weigh so much, by the time I finished one outpost, I was feeling too exhausted to even think about another one. It's unnecessarily complex, tedious, and serves no purpose. I think it’s specifically this element that finally made me quit the game.

7. The cultural differences between the main factions are also very badly written. And there is no originality. It feels like Bethesda just copies them from different pop culture elements. The United Colonies feels more like Star Trek, the Freestar Collective is a poor copy of Firefly, and Neon is a generic cyberpunk city (more like a small town). I get that they wanted each faction to feel unique, but they are so different that at times it feels difficult to accept that they are part of the lore of the same game.

8. There is absolutely no reason for Starfield (or any Microsoft game) to cost as much as it does, not when the money is not going to the game devs and is just profit for the corporation who are going to fire the devs anyway.

[h2]The Average:[/h2]

1. The music is not bad, it’s not great. It’s fine. It doesn’t fill me with awe, neither does it feel epic in any sense. But otherwise it fits the setting.

2. Unlike many others I don’t mind the lack of advanced alien cultures. The Outer Worlds did a good job at world building without them, but Starfield failed to make their world interesting enough to make up for that.

3. Like the rest of the game, the combay is excruciatingly mediocre. You might enjoy it for a few hours. There is a nice variety of guns that can be upgraded, but it all gets repititive rather fast. It also doesn't help that the special powers are rather lacklustre and there are no interesting features to invest in like VATS or Mass Effect's bionic powers.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

If you want the experience of casually travelling throughout the galaxy, or if you, like me, have read the Expanse recently and wanted a taste of space, Starfield is fine. Just don’t expect a good RPG. It is an overpriced mess and a severe downgrade from all past Bethesda titles.

Bethesda has been moving towards radiant quests since Skyrim. They are not fun. They encourage lazy writing, and their only purpose seems to be lengthening the game. They add absolutely nothing to the lore or the narrative. To those who like good writing in RPGs, it's a slap in the face. And despite heavy criticism against them, Bethesda seems to be doubling down on them. So Starfield doesn't make me hopeful for the next Bethesda game at all.

Final verdict: 05 / 10

text:
Since buying into the early access of this game two years ago, I've been keeping a close eye on the development and it's unfortunate to say that the progression of what could have been an amazing game in an under-served genre has found itself in a ditch. Like many other reviews have already commented, the AI pathfinding is buggy, there is a lack of endgame content, basic agriculture like crop rotation and ploughing is buggy and fails to work half the time, etc. etc. This isn't what my review will touch on; it has already been established that many fundamental issues aren't being addressed.

What I want to touch on is the current state of the studio Slavic Magic and moreso the narrative around Greg the developer. This isn't a hate review of Greg, as I still somewhat believe in him, but this belief is slowly draining each day. Now for those who bought in at the start, you would've known Greg as the sole developer behind Manor Lords; if you played at the beginning of early access, you would've been hit with a pop up detailing this fact each time you launched the game. This is honestly commendable for having delivered what more or less is a similar version of the Manor Lords today save for the modern version having a few more bells and whistles back in 2024 as a single developer. Awe inspiring actually and has created this layer of mysticism surrounding Greg. Compound this with disgruntled players from the Paradox and Total War franchises and you create almost a messianic figure in Greg. He is our saviour, a single man set out to do what these triple A studios couldn't and we should all be blessed for having the opportunity to play this game in early access. 

However, this is no longer the case. We are no longer dealing with just Greg at this point but an entire studio he has built. Slavic Magic has dedicated 3d modellers, mappers, artists, coders, etc. it's not just Greg plugging away at it on his own. On top of that, we have Hooded Horse, an already successful and established double A publisher in this genre of Medieval games aiding in advertisement and other avenues Slavic Magic no longer needs to worry about for a successful launch. Yet, despite this, we are still faced with bugs and issues that were there on day 1. I understand game development doesn't happen overnight, I understand Greg was once working at this alone and thus had to balance development, publishing, and a plethora of other factors, but come on, it has been two years how are we just now adding in stone churches? 

Unfortunately, a vast majority of the community is still under the influence of Greg's messianic tale. If you go onto the Manor Lords discord and levy any criticism, constructive or otherwise, at the project, you will be met with angry fans spilling vitriol for daring to say otherwise. I'll even wager under this review there will be angry believers offended by my audacity. This is not a healthy place to be for a community and will only lead to death spirals that eventually leads to the community becoming nothing more than a husk. It is what it is and I don't blame Greg of course because how could he anticipate this success(they've made over 80 million in revenue btw) and the mix of fans that elevated him to such a position, but holy some of you need to see reality for what it is. 

If you're looking to buy this game, I wouldn't recommend it for its current price tag of 40 USD. It's a decent game for a couple of hours of play, but only really that much as there is no real endgame and it gets stale rather fast. It definitely won't replace any Total War or Paradox games that you are disgruntled with if you are coming from those franchises, so I would leave those expectations at the door despite what game journos are saying. Hopefully Slavic Magic will come out of this stump and we will get a coherent path towards 1.0.

text:
Payday 3 isn't a terrible game. It introduces some genuinely good ideas and improves parts of the formula, but it often feels like it was developed by a team that didn't fully understand what made Payday so memorable.
Comparing Payday 3 to a game with over 10 years of updates isn't, by itself, why it has so many negative reviews. The lack of content is not the only part of the problem. In my opinion, the biggest issue is that Payday 3 lost much of the identity that made the franchise stand out.

[h1]What Payday 3 Got Right[/h1]

[h2]Maskless Stealth[/h2]
Being able to complete parts of a heist without putting on your mask is an excellent addition. You can now perform actions like picking up keycards, hacking phones, cameras, or computers while still blending in. It allows you to push stealth much further before , making heists feel more "strategic".

[h2]Remote Camera Hacking[/h2]
Another welcome improvement is the ability to hack cameras remotely. In Payday 2 you had find the security room to access the entire system. In Payday 3, hacking a single camera gives you access to all of them, removing unnecessary busywork..

[h2]Moving Cameras[/h2]
Security cameras are no longer fixed in place. They now rotate and cover different areas, creating more opportunities to move through blind spots if you're patient enough.

[h2]More Natural Guards[/h2]
One of the biggest frustrations with Payday 2 stealth was how guards seemed to have eyes in the back of their heads. In Payday 3, they behave much more naturally, detecting you only when they actually have line of sight. This makes stealth significantly less frustrating.

[h2]Public, Private and Secure Areas[/h2]
The new area system works perfectly with maskless stealth. Entering a secure area usually results in a guard escorting you out instead of immediately failing the stealth. Truly private areas remain dangerous, where being spotted has real consequences. This makes mistakes less punishing while still rewarding careful play.

[h2]Better Special Enemies[/h2]
The new Nader does exactly what a special enemy should do: force you to adapt. When it appears, you have to reposition or deal with it before it throws its smoke grenade.
The Shield also received meaningful improvements. Regular SWAT units now actively use it as cover.
[strike] I FORGOT ABOUT TECHIE AND THE SWAT VAN [/strike]

[h1]The Problems[/h1]

[h2]A Contradictory Lockpicking System[/h2]
The lockpicking minigame is a clear improvement over simply holding a button. However, the game also includes a skill that completely bypasses this mechanic, making its existence feel questionable.

On top of that, the input handling is poorly implemented. Since there's no small delay after completing the minigame, it's very easy to click one extra time and accidentally fire your weapon, ruining an entire stealth run.

[h2]Oversimplified Preplanning[/h2]
Many of the old Assets have been moved into the in-game store, hidden away in a menu that many players won't even notice the first time they open it.

They're also consumable now. If a specific Asset isn't available, the only option is to replay heists until it eventually drops. After grinding for one, there's very little incentive to actually use it when it disappears after a single run.

[h2]Oversimplified Skills[/h2]
Most skills are nothing more than small numerical bonuses. Very few skills fundamentally change how you play, which greatly reduces build diversity.

[h2]Build Variety[/h2]
Builds have lost much of the variety that made Payday 2 so enjoyable.
In stealth, the difference often comes down to equipping a suppressor. In loud gameplay, there are also very few meaningful choices that significantly change your playstyle.
In Payday 2, Perk Decks completely transformed how you approached the game.

Crew Chief focused on supporting the entire team by increasing health, damage absorption and stamina.

Grinder and Stoic encouraged health-based builds, working especially well alongside skills like Hostage Taker.

Anarchist and Armorer focused on armor while synergizing with Berserker, rewarding players for staying at low health in a classic high-risk, high-reward playstyle.

Rogue and Hacker revolved around dodge builds, often combined with critical hits and suppressed weapons.

In Payday 3, that level of variety has almost completely disappeared.

[h2]Always Online[/h2]
This is, in my opinion, the game's biggest flaw.

People often defend it by saying that "it's an industry standard now," but that argument doesn't hold much weight if the system itself isn't reliable. More importantly, it's not as if creating a game without this level of online dependency is impossible.

The problem isn't simply requiring an internet connection to start a match. Nearly every menu interaction depends on communicating with the servers.
Buying weapons, installing modifications, or even changing your loadout requires a successful server response. I've personally had multiple occasions where purchases or equipment changes simply failed because the servers were unstable or didn't respond.

This dependency adds nothing to the player experience while creating unnecessary frustration.

[h2]Solo Mode[/h2]
For a long time, the game didn't even include a proper solo mode. Players had to create online lobbies just to play alone.

Even today, Solo Mode is still labeled as Beta.

[h2]Loss of Identity[/h2]
In my opinion, this is Payday 3's biggest problem and one of the main reasons so many players walked away from the game.
The franchise's identity was never just about robbing banks—it was about how those heists could be approached.

In Payday 2, individual heists had their own personality. Big Bank allowed you to either bring in a massive drill using a crane or melt through the vault ceiling with thermite. During stealth, you even had to use a finger to bypass the biometric scanner.

San Martín Bank let you choose a loud entry where Vlad's brother-in-law smashed through the bank entrance with a car.

Golden Grin Casino allowed you to upgrade the laser drill itself by improving its cooling system, increasing water capacity, strengthening the laser, or even mounting sentry guns on top of it.

These details made every heist feel unique.

The same was true for builds, Perk Decks, skills, and the Asset system.
In Payday 3, much of that personality has disappeared. The systems have been simplified, and the differences between playstyles have largely vanished.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Over the past few years, Payday 3 has received several updates fixing many of the launch heists, especially those that mostly consisted of standing inside circles while waiting for timers to finish.
Those improvements were necessary, but they don't address the core issue.

In my opinion, the reason many players haven't returned to Payday 3 isn't simply because it lacks content. If that were the only problem, adding more heists would have solved it.
Payday 2 is still played every day despite no longer receiving new heists. Most players simply replay the same heists because they're memorable and offer unique approaches.

That's exactly what Payday 3 still hasn't managed to recover.
The game may eventually become much better, but adding content is far easier than restoring the identity that made Payday what it was.

[h3]DO NOT RECOMMEND[/h3]
If you're a fan of the previous Payday games and expect a natural evolution of the series, you'll probably find a sequel that simplified many of the systems that originally gave the franchise its identity.

New players may still enjoy it at first. Eventually, though, you'll likely understand why so many people still point to Payday 2 "10 years of content" as the reason for its success, when, in my opinion, the real reason goes much deeper than that.

text:
Given how hyped this game is, I would like to give you an in-depth analysis of both its positive and negative aspects and explain to you why I don’t recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 for most players. I will break this review down into the Good, the Bad and the Ugly:

The Good:
Let’s start with what makes this game truly shine.
Characters. You’ll get up to 10 recruitable companions with lots of unique dialogues and (for the most part) their own personal quests, some of which fantastically written, revealing rich origin stories including deep character development. Add stellar voice acting on top of all that and you get a highly immersive and memorable experience! 
Motion capture animations. Another reason why this game and its characters are so immersive is the motion capture animations. I think I’ve never experienced so many characters in a single video game coming so vividly and iconically to life as in bg3. Again, the voice acting adds massively to that.
Adjusting Dungeons & Dragons rules. For those of you who are unfamiliar with the original pen and paper game, it’s extremely unbalanced, especially when comparing the different classes to play. In the community, it’s widely known that there is a huge power gap between spellcaster and martial classes which gradually widens from middle to late levels. Larian studios apparently learned from DnD players homebrewing and elegantly solved this by cutting the maximum level down to 12 (which is btw how most tabletop DnD campaigns are being played) and redesigning certain classes.
Soundtrack. It’s all you could ask for in an RPG: epic during intense moments, soft during emotional moments, dreamy during exploration and overall fantastical.

The Bad:
As cool and amazing as the good stuff sounds, there is a lot of bad stuff we need to address here.
Tutorial is very lackluster for gamers with zero DnD experience. If you’re completely new to DnD, you should probably stop here because this game won’t even teach you the basics properly. Fortunately, I have DnD experience and know the rules of 5th edition, upon which this game is based, so it was no problem for me. However, I can see a newbie getting steam rolled repeatedly without knowing why simply because they haven’t been taught well.
Difficulty is all over the place in this game. I’ve only played on balanced difficulty so perhaps this doesn’t apply as much to other difficulty levels but don’t expect a linear increase of difficulty overall. Act 1 (Char level 1-6) felt to me like walking through a minefield. Act 2 (Char level 6-10) on the other hand felt like your usual gaming experience. Most battles were moderately challenging with a few boss battles that demanded more strategic thinking. Finally, in act 3 (Char level 10-12), most battles became trivial with combatants at much lower levels than your party and subpar gear you could already loot/buy in act 1. Even some boss battles didn’t impose that much of a challenge.
Just one bad decision could screw up your whole playthrough which is devastating in an extremely long game like this (more on that later). I had to basically start over after 35 hours because I realized after a quick internet research that due to one single misjudgment I’ve completely locked myself out of recruiting Karlach, the companion who I was looking forward to the most and wanted to romance, although I haven’t even met her yet. And that's just one of many examples of how you can unknowingly and irreversibly maneuver yourself into a very unpleasant situation, which is why I advise against approaching this game blindly, as I did and as is usually the case for me with RPGs.
Mini games with mechanics not to expect in an RPG game. There have been a few occasions when I wondered whether I purchased the wrong game because it suddenly deviated from its turn based RPG formula and turned into a completely different game with completely different gameplay mechanics and those are NOT skippable. Maybe this is a me thing but when I purchase a game I expect it to be what the description says and not surprise me with in built mandatory mini games that stop the momentum and force a different gaming experience upon me.
This game is fricking looooooooooooong! It took me 220+ hours to finish it, NOT including the 35 hours I replayed. Moreover, I skipped some content at the very end of the game, just to get over with it faster. Now you might be thinking: if there’s a lot of exploration and story to dive into then that kind of length would be natural. However, about half of my playtime went into sometimes boring, sometimes infuriating downtime that could have been greatly reduced if it wasn’t for bad game design. More on that in the “Ugly”- part.

The Ugly:
The ugly parts aren’t nearly as buzzkill as the bad ones but annoying to say the least.
Level design is counter intuitive and unnecessarily prolongs the game with confusion. Most of the larger buildings like palaces, temples and forts look as if a drunk architect built them. There is close to zero consistency in terms of layout and some pathways and connections look completely out of place. I guess they tried to avoid sameness while providing intriguing playgrounds for specific battles but in the end, they just turned out confusing. I’ve lost count of how many times I got lost in a place I’ve walked past several times before because of this goofy design.
Inventory management is clunky. RPG veterans know all too well how much stuff is piling up over the course of a full playthrough when there is loot literally everywhere and it’s no different in bg3. Some games offer you search and filter options for easier management but not this game. Although you have separate pouches for alchemy, keys and food, if you want any sort of order in your inventory, you have to drag and drop every single item at a time. The “add to wares” - function isn’t helpful either because you’d still have to click on every single item in order to use it. May as well drag and drop when you’re trading. Far from elegant and again, something that unnecessarily prolongs the game.
Lootable vessels are everywhere! Why is that bad, you may ask? Because almost all of them are empty. I started this game looking into every single lootable vessel I laid eyes upon until I realized I haven’t found anything, even after opening the 100th or so. So I started using the hotkey that highlights all important lootable places on screen and went with this for the rest of the game. However, I still occasionally opened “unimportant” vessels out of boredom and to my surprise I found an important key in act 2 in one of those. So not only does the game drown you in loot spaces of which most are empty but also it misleads you in falsely believing you could save time by ignoring them and focusing on the “important stuff”! Yet another way you can waste hours and hours of playtime in a frustrating way.
Traps. It seems like traps in bg3 serve the sole purpose of wasting your time and resources. They’re not puzzles as you might think, they’re simply hindrances that require you to pass an ability check. Otherwise, you’ll have to suck up the damage. So it comes down to resource management only. You won’t get a feeling of intellectual achievement from interacting with them, but rather annoyance.
Line of sight isn’t always clear. Sometimes, I wondered what obstructed my attempt of throwing a weapon or a ranged spell at an enemy because when I adjust the camera to my character’s pov, I could see a clear line to my target. Maybe the programming is a bit clunky here or I missed something but if it’s the latter, they could have at least highlighted the object that gets in my way for better understanding. Also, for some reason ranged spells that deal damage in a straight line don’t work over stairs. Can someone explain to me why I can’t aim my spell slightly upwards/downwards?

If you made it this far, congratulations and thank you very much for your attention!

text:
Recent update has sapped some of the fun with the game. The health pool on bosses do not respect your time. The game in general does not respect your time. 

You lose exp on dying. The maps themselves don't respect your time as they have countless dead ends and piles of rubble that make you walk a big circle around the level. It makes backtracking a chore and completely uncovering the maps a long process. I understand that is a fundamental part of the game and I can deal with running around the levels but in conjunction with the other current issues these minor annoyances are exacerbated.

The game has a ton of content and a pretty good build system but there are legacy systems that need to be smoothed out. Dodge has been added to the game years after the game was developed. It has been made to be a mandatory ability if you don't want to quickly hit a wall with the bosses. The issue with this is the game was not initially designed with dodge in mind. The dodge is clunky and mushy with a long cooldown. 

A lot of early boss fights take place in relatively tight arenas with every other mob having ground effects. The boss arenas and some of their attacks clearly suffer from dodge being added. 

The game is currently over-tuned with one-shots being the way you will die 95% of the time. It is not uncommon to die with absolutely no idea what killed you or how to defend because there is no combat log.

The early tough fights often force you to hit-and-run bosses that can one shot you and have such massive health pools in fights that even easy ones are painfully slow right now. I have sat there and face tanked a boss while just holding down the attack button and surf on my second monitor because it will take 5 minutes to kill it with the currently bloated health pools. You will be destroying the trash mobs on the way to the bosses which makes it difficult to see weaknesses in your build because the the vast majority of deaths are boss or elite mobs one-shotting you with very little feedback on wtf just happened to you.

These are not game breaking. Things can be tuned for normal players not the ones with 7000 hours in the game telling everyone to get good. Vets recommend "play a better build". Sorry but if I have to play some youtuber's build in order to progress and have fun that is not a great sign. 

The gameplay feels like Last Epoch forced into POE2 gameplay with neither identity really working currently.

Attempting to discuss this or any other criticisms in the forum is met with a dev (instead of a badly needed community manager) that simply ignores and talks down to people trying to give feedback. 

If you want to ask questions or point out issues you are having after you've bought the main game and every DLC then have fun being insulted by an angry crowd of people who have played the game a decade non-stop and a Dev who is condescending and insulting people.

I've never mentioned a dev in a review but the way Crate is responding to criticism leaves me feeling dubious about any changes being made.

The game isn't by nature a bad game but currently you have to really work for the fun. I will update this in the future as the game progresses but right now it is tough to recommend with the response to some of the criticisms are outright hostility.

Hopefully I can delete this review in the future and replace it with something more positive but for right now thumbs down for current state of the game.

text:
I'd like to say I enjoyed Return to Monkey Island and for a decent portion of it, I did. However the game is built upon two assumptions:

1. You're a Monkey Island fan.
2. You want to see the series come to a satisfying conclusion.

As such, a lot of the game is built around old tropes of the series and continuously makes references back to old jokes and events from previous titles. This is fine in and of itself but something that I found made Monkey Island 1-3 continuously interesting and fulfilling was the willingness to expand its own world and venture into new territories.

RtMI doesn't really tread any new ground aside from a few new locations in the latter half of the game. The story is pretty much beating a dead horse and hoping something exciting happens. And when nothing exciting happens we're supposed to sit back and laugh at ourselves for being so gullible as to expect the creators to do something satisfying with what is supposed to be the ultimate love letter to their series.

Also, I'm not a fan of being given hints. Yes, it speeds the game up when you're stumped. But this is a Monkey Island game. You're supposed to sit scratching your head at least a few times thinking "What the hell do they want me to do here?" until you eventually rub the right items together and bam, puzzle solved. Giving a book of hints just takes away all the satisfaction of eventually coming to the answer by yourself.

I can see what the creators were going for here. A little homage to their body of work and the nostalgia that the series evokes. I get it.

But that's not an excuse to be lazy.

text:
[h1]Monkey Island: The Made-For-TV Cast Reunion Special[/h1]

Have you ever watched one of those made-for-TV specials where they reunite the cast from a popular TV show many decades after the show ended?  You know how some of those specials feel like they are just an excuse to get the original cast in the same room again, don't have a meaningful script, and just end up being a melancholy "callback to better days" where the cast members are constantly winking into the camera, reminiscing about things that happened in the original series, and are repeatedly saying things like "Wow, it's been a long time" or "We're not as young as we used to be" instead of creating an enjoyable new chapter in the series?

Well, that's basically what this game is...

Conceptually, I don't know who the devs were catering to here.  They offer a Casual Mode with fewer puzzles for newcomers, and then they offer a Hard Mode for veterans which is still weak compared to the "normal" difficulty of the previous games.  Also, in a rather strange design choice, they decided to cut out some of the game's script and hide it behind a somewhat hard-to-find Writer's Cut option in the Settings menu seemingly because, according to the option's description, they thought there was too much "blather" in the original draft of the script.  (I played Writer's Cut and thought there was still not enough dialog.)  No idea why they decided to do that because the writing is what I was here for.  Then it feels like they later decided there was not enough "game" in Casual Mode and needed give people something else to do.  So they added a set of collectibles to find in the form of trivia cards which ask you questions...about the old games and the out-of-universe development process at LucasArts.  Not sure who those trivia cards are directed at because Casual Mode players probably won't know the answers, and Hard Mode fans would probably have preferred more actual puzzles.

On the subject of the writing, the comedy mostly is gone.  (Even with Writer's Cut Mode and the extended Hard Mode enabled.)  I maybe chuckled once or twice, but that's it.  In fact, Guybrush is uncharacteristically cruel in many places which took away from whatever humor there was.  The traditional insult swordfighting from other games is only briefly referenced in places and is not a playable part of the game.  There are way too many callbacks to the old games, and it felt like a chore to remember, "Oh yeah, I think I recall that thing that happened in MI2, etc." just to enjoy the story of this game.  Also, even the funniest returning characters aren't that funny in this game.  ([spoiler]Stan isn't actively trying to scam anyone and spends most of the game in jail.  Murray isn't as funny as he usually is and honestly doesn't say a lot.  Elaine wins the award for being the most strange though: Instead of being the longsuffering wife who is always bailing Guybrush out, she acts more like his mother and sort of pats him on the head and patronizes him even when he's being malicious.[/spoiler])  Many of the supporting characters and villains also just unceremoniously disappear at certain points in the game - which was odd.  Another thing that I didn't like is that the entire story had this weird, Disney-fied, Kathleen-Kennedy-era Indiana Jones/Star Wars feel to it where it was all ultra-sterile and by-the-numbers, but then it tried to go in awkward "heartfelt" directions even when it was uncalled for.  Finally, the [spoiler]Boybrush[/spoiler] story framing seriously broke immersion with frequent, meaningless interludes, and the whole "washed-up Guybrush" theme was rather depressing (once again feeling like Kathleen Kennedy's Indy and Star Wars movies).

On the subject of the ending, I had already braced myself for the usual trademark Bad Ron Gilbert Ending, but this ending feels particularly bad because it's like Gilbert just gave up at the end and went home.  In fact, after all of the promises about "fixing" the Monkey Island 2 ending, this game not only failed to convincingly write itself out of the MI2 ending debacle, but in many aspects it wrote itself back into an even worse quandary in its own ending.  Also, it actually destroys a lot of the long-running gags in the series by tying up loose ends that should have never been addressed.  (Like [spoiler]revealing the Voodoo Lady's real name, actually showing what appears to be the Secret of Monkey Island (unless they do another retcon sometime)[/spoiler], etc.)

And no, I don't like the graphics and think they look like cheap ClipArt.  That's about all I'm going to say about it because it's a subjective thing, but I would have preferred them use artwork in line with Curse of Monkey Island.

In summary, I dove into this game because I wanted to enjoy myself and laugh along.  Once I finished though, I simply didn't feel happy because of the overall downer tone and the lack of what made the previous games great.  At this point, I'm trying to decide if this game or Escape from Monkey Island is the worst in the series, and I'm thinking that Return probably is in the bottom spot (even in spite of the Monkey Kombat mess from Escape).  Monkey Island lives and dies by the quality of the writing, and I feel like Return had worse writing than every other game in the series.  Really a shame.

I used to love this game. Elite Dangerous was once one of the best space simulators ever made.

I still remember the wonder I felt the first time I launched into space, jumping from system to system, staring at the full explorable galaxy map, and setting off on long voyages into the vast unknown. I played as a hauler, moving goods from one location to another. It was simple, but deeply fulfilling. As I built my reputation, I earned better parts, more cargo space, better ships, higher payouts, and the ability to travel to distant systems.

Back then, the progression felt rewarding. I remember starting with tiny payouts of only a few thousand credits, and by the end of my last playthrough a few years ago, I was earning millions per mission. It felt like my time and effort mattered.

I recently reinstalled the game hoping to relive that nostalgia, but unfortunately, I was very disappointed. This once-beloved game has become painfully grindy. Now even allied factions only seem to offer a couple hundred thousand credits instead of the millions they used to. Many of the missions require you to spend credits to purchase or locate goods yourself, which takes away from the simple hauling gameplay I loved.

The old-school hauling experience feels like it is gone. I have a Type-9 Heavy with around 640 cargo space, but I often end up hauling maybe 200 goods for what feels like scraps. The reward just does not match the ship, the effort, or the time invested anymore.

I had heard people say the developers drove this game into the ground, but I didn't want to believe it. Sadly, after coming back, I understand why people feel this way.

Goodbye, Elite Dangerous. You are the ex I used to love.

text:
I'm a huge fan of the original Resident Evil 4, so take this review with a grain of salt, I suppose. But this game does not need to exist. The original game is still fantastic and didn't need a glow up. The only improvements this remake boasts are cosmetic. Ada's new look and voice is an improvement. She actually reads as Asian now, and I can believe she could do spy work in this new outfit over the old cocktail dress. 

I think I prefer Ashley's new look too, and I like the subtlety in how they develop her love for Leon. The way she looks at him when he catches her for the first time is a nice touch. As much goofy fun as it is when she propositions Leon on the back of the jet ski in the original, it's more authentic that she'd instead constantly hint they should keep teaming up in the future. I like this new take.

But not all of the cosmetic changes are positive. Leon still looks and sounds cooler in the original. Krauser DEFINTIELY sounds cooler, and so does Sadler. And Ramon Salazar is exponentially more entertaining in the original. I have over a thousand hours in the original game, and I never skip Ramon's cut scenes. I just 100 percented the remake, and I skip his cut scenes every time now, have been since the middle of the second play through. He just isn't entertaining any more. Resident Evil 4's story is ridiculous, but that's its charm, and that's what fans love about it. The new game devs robbed this Japanese fever dream of all its personality, and now it's just another run of the mill shooter. And that would be fine, except the remake basically impeaches the existence of the original. Those new to the franchise will most likely play this newer, shinier version and skip the superior original altogether.

Beyond all that, the game's pretty buggy. Grenades don't do lethal damage, they're just stun grenades that can't insta-kill plagas. Incendiaries don't exist anymore, odd choice. Leon's movement control is pretty sloppy. It's a gamble whether you'll actually make a knife attack when the game gives you the contextual prompt, so you eventually stop making them altogether in favor of burning more ammunition on an attack that will actually land. And whoever decided it was a good idea to give the knife a health bar should be fired. Possibly out of a cannon.

All in all, you'll probably enjoy this game. It's fun. But of course it is. They just copy-pasted one of the greatest games of all time and resold it. If you're a fan of the first one, you'll probably enjoy this game enough to justify picking it up on a ten dollar sale like I did. But definitely don't pay full price.

text:
Not a terrible game. But since I lost interest after about 10 hours is is not worth the money. It's main problems are:
- Terrible controls: It's obviously a console game but most console games that are ported to PC do a way better job at adopting controls. (for example: I lost count of how ofter I accidently left the controls of the space ship and got out of my pilot chair because this is the same button as aiming at an enemy ship...for some reason someone thought that would be a good idea)
- Lack of motivation: While there is lots of stuff to do (exploration, ground combat, space combat, base building etc.) there is little reason to do any of it. The story and characters don't provide hooks and frankly I got bored after about 10 hours.
- The core gameplay elements are mediocre in quality. Ground combat (at normal difficulty, haven't tried others yet) is a bullet sponge shooting at bullet sponges, space combat suffers massively from poor controls and from the fast travel system. Base building is a grind with little revard that is locked behind perks that are locked behind other perks. Throughout that grind the player is mostly fighting the controls of the game or pressing the "always walk" button and mining minerals in between fast travelling.

Also the game design itself leans heavily into loading screen watching:
- fast travel to quest planet/station. (loading screen)
(-possibly a random encounter in space in which you are droped right on top of the enemies at the start rather than some distance away which would allow to use the elements in the game such as stealth, scanner, weapons with great range etc.)
- Land on planet (cutscene/loading screen)
- walk to quest marker and shoot bullet sponges. (fight against lack of QoL elements when it comes to inventory management)
- fast travel back to hand in quest (loading screen)
- fast travel to merchant A to sell stuff (2 loading screens, travelling + opening the door to the merchant)
- fast travel to merchant B to sell other stuff because merchant A only buys some stuff. (2 loading screens)
- fast travel to merchant C to sell more of the same stuff because merchant B had not enough money. (another 2 loading screens)
- get a new quest and repeat


The game could vastly improve if controls were better and QoL features were added such as better inventory management and beeing able to sell everything directly from inside the ship when landing in a major settlement. Add a combat overhaul mod on top of that and improve fast travelling and (random) encounters and the result would likely be a fun game.
It's not a terrible game, it's just not worth my time as there are far better games out there to play.

I may return in the future to try a modded version of the game.

text:
Unfortunately, X4 just misses about every possible beat; as wide as a medium-sized pond, as shallow as a swamp.

Setting annoying bugs aside, the whole game feels rather lackluster and is normally gated behind some form of mechanic.

[b]Let's use mining as an example.[/b]

There's plenty of guides out there explaining how mining works, right from soloing asteroid feels all the way to self-sustained mining fleets complete with stations. Sounds great. Problem is, to get past the manual phase and into automation requires your pilots to be of a specific skill level, that level, even with mods, is inherently slow. So let's say you assign a miner (Solid/Gas, doesn't matter) to your station, they need to be a specific skill requirement to do prospecting. You can't have them locally automine, because they can't find the right rocks.

Research. That's another fun topic: requires resources delivering to your station, but it's another tedious and slow process that requires money and ridiculous amounts of patience.

There is also no story in X4, albeit a very loose one. As you progress from the game, regardless of start, you will slowly unveil (or be forced) to have specific events happen. There is a particular event in this game where, no matter what, you end up with a free station. Just no explanation, poof, it appears - do some minor annoying side quests, here's a station.

The bugs are few and far between, but some can be quite gamebreaking. An example is when you have a relief Captain aboard your fighter towards the start of a new run. Sometimes when you ask them to get space-bound, they just randomly clip into the station and get stuck. Very annoying.

I think apart from all that, the game is relatively good looking, has decent soundscapes and for the more patient player, probably rewarding.

To me, X4 is just very lackluster in a lot of areas and I constantly find myself thinking "when does the fun begin?" and that is a bad sign from a game. Sorry Egosoft, please do better on X5.

text:
I went into Starfield expecting a Bethesda game, and that is exactly what I got—for better and for worse.

At its best, I absolutely loved it. The faction stories, companions, cities, strange planets, political conflicts, ship collecting, exploration, and endless little side stories gave me the same feeling I get from Fallout and The Elder Scrolls. I became invested in the United Colonies, joined the Freestar Rangers, infiltrated the Crimson Fleet, worked my way through Ryujin Industries, explored House Va’ruun society, and gradually uncovered the mystery behind the Artifacts and the Unity.

Despite all the criticism surrounding the game, Starfield still felt unmistakably like Bethesda to me. It is a huge sandbox filled with interesting characters, factions, lore, moral decisions, and distractions. I enjoyed inhabiting this universe, and there were many nights when I intended to play for an hour and ended up staying for several.

I also understand why the game divided people. Space travel is heavily segmented by menus, loading screens, docking animations, elevators, and transitions. You do not freely fly from a planet’s surface into orbit in the way many people hoped. The underlying technology clearly has limits, and the game never completely delivers the seamless space-exploration fantasy its setting suggests.

That bothered me less than it bothered many other players. I knew this was still built around Bethesda’s existing engine and design structure. Once I accepted that, it felt like a traditional Bethesda RPG spread across a galaxy rather than a true space simulator—and I was fine with that.

Unfortunately, this was also one of the most technically frustrating games I have ever finished.

I encountered bugs that disrupted faction finales, companion quests, DLC missions, travel, quest markers, NPC behaviour, docking states, and follower AI. One major faction finale became impossible because a defensive battery began flying away faster than my ship could approach it. I eventually had to complete the quest with console commands, which caused me to miss most of its ending.

During the Terran Armada content, an essential robot companion disappeared inside a location I could no longer access. My regular companion was stranded there as well, and the quest could not continue until another mission’s loading transition finally caused the robot to reappear.

There were several other moments when objectives vanished, NPCs failed to appear, locations did not become selectable, or scripts simply stopped progressing.

The most damaging result was that I eventually stopped trusting the game.

Whenever an objective was unclear, I no longer wondered what clue I had missed or what puzzle I was supposed to solve. I wondered whether the quest had broken again. Even normal moments became frustrating because I could not tell whether I was misunderstanding the directions or dealing with another technical failure.

That is a terrible state for an RPG to put the player in. Instead of thinking about the story and the world, I was searching forums, reloading old saves, experimenting with console commands, and worrying that every workaround might break something else later.

Yes, Bethesda games have always been buggy. At this point, buying one and expecting a flawless experience would be optimistic to the point of comedy. The community will inevitably create mods that repair many of these problems, just as it has for Bethesda’s previous games.

But “the modders will fix it” should not excuse major quests and paid expansions breaking years after release.

What makes this so frustrating is that underneath the technical problems is a game I genuinely enjoyed.

The UC Vanguard storyline was a highlight, with a strong mystery and some of the best world-building in the game. The Freestar Rangers gave me the space-western adventure I expected from Akila City. The Crimson Fleet and SysDef campaign offered meaningful choices and an excellent setup, even though its finale broke for me. Ryujin’s corporate espionage story had too much forced stealth for my taste, but it still offered an interesting look at Neon’s politics and corruption.

The main Constellation story becomes much more compelling once the Starborn and Unity enter the picture. I liked the philosophical idea behind the ending, although I was disappointed that the game never truly explains who created the Artifacts, the temples, or the Unity. It hints at mysterious “Creators,” but the central question remains deliberately unanswered.

The companions were also among the strongest parts of the experience. Their personal stories gave the adventure emotional weight, and the major choice involving the Lodge and the Eye was genuinely effective. Losing a companion permanently made the universe feel more consequential than I expected.

Shattered Space offered a more concentrated, handcrafted Bethesda experience. Exploring Va’ruun society, its religion, political houses, and ruined capital was interesting, and I appreciated having a major storyline centred on one location instead of constantly jumping between systems.

Terran Armada had some entertaining ideas and impressive encounters, but it was also where I experienced some of my worst quest and companion bugs. That made it difficult to recommend as paid content, even though I enjoyed portions of the story.

Starfield is difficult for me to review because my emotional reaction and my practical recommendation are pulling in opposite directions.

I loved playing it. It gave me the familiar Bethesda experience I wanted, and I enjoyed it about as much as I enjoyed exploring Fallout and Skyrim. I liked its world, writing, factions, companions, atmosphere, and sense of discovery. Even after all the frustration, I am glad I played it.

But I cannot ignore how much time I spent repairing the game instead of playing it.

This is a wonderful Bethesda RPG trapped inside an unreliable piece of software. Players willing to save constantly, install community fixes, search for workarounds, and occasionally use the console may find an enormous game worth loving. Anyone expecting a polished, dependable experience should be very cautious.

Recommended—with a very large asterisk.

On the positive side, ship building is very fun. I also enjoyed base building far more than I expected.

One confession: I always make sure my ships have enough toilets so none of the crew has to wait. If that makes me weird... so be it.

Starfield is one of those games that is almost great. It has flashes of brilliance mixed with repetitive systems and unrealized ideas. Despite its flaws, I enjoyed my time with it.

7/10. Worth playing, especially if you can pick it up on sale.

text:
I like the Spider-Man franchise, watched all of the movies and played some of the games. This game became one of my all-time favourite games after I finished it, with one of the best stories about the wall-crawler I've ever seen.

The gameplay of this game is a lot of fun. The web swinging and traversal in general are some of the best in any Spider-Man game, there's some stealth sections and puzzles to break up the combat and you have a wide variety of gadgets to use against your enemies.

The combat is what I enjoy the most about this game. Enemies come in a few types, including gun-wielding ones, jetpack ones, big ones that absorb damage unless if you stun them. The enemies can actually hurt you well if you don't use perfect dodges and your equipment well, and the game might take a while to get used to but once you do, it's a lot of fun.

There's also a LOT of side content that makes up a lot of this game, things like combat arenas featuring waves of enemies, collectibles etc, typical open world game stuff. It's done well here imo and it's satisfying when you max out Spider-Man's upgrades.

The game also includes quite a few bosses which feature familiar faces like Doc Ock, Rhino, Scorpion to lesser known villains like Shocker and Mr. Negative. The boss fights are quite fun but lean on the easy side once you play the game well at least for me.

The story is one of the best I've seen not just in Spider-Man media but games in general. The voice acting is amazing (no pun intended), the plot twists are well-done and some parts of the story definitely gave me emotions especially the ending.

The dlcs are decent but I found them to be on the unforgiving side especially the second and third ones. Still, if you enjoyed the base game I recommend playing them as well.

I can sing a lot of praise for this game but it's not without its fair share of bad parts. The stealth sections happen way too often and can get boring, some fights are badly designed and the game can be confusing to progress through at times, but these are overall minor compared to the enjoyment I had playing it
